summary.title: Spice.ai OSS v2.0.0
summary.description: Spice is a portable, open-source runtime for fast, last-mile SQL query, search, and AI inference.

diagrams.title: Data + AI Runtime (Local/Network)

data.name: Spice Runtime
data.description: Rust daemon exposing SQL, Flight, OpenAI-compatible, MCP, and Iceberg APIs with embedded accelerators. v2.0 adds DDL support (CREATE/DROP TABLE) for Iceberg and Cayenne catalogs, async query materialization to object storage, distributed ingestion, URL Tables (opt-in SSRF surface), SMB/NFS data connectors, and acceleration snapshot management API.

threats.title: Bypass data source AuthN/AuthZ
threats.description: Users with access to the Spice runtime APIs can access information from the data source either via federated SQL query or through queries on a configured accelerator, potentially getting access to data they don't normally have access to.
threats.mitigation:
This is an expected behavior of the system. Spice can be used by design to provide access to data without needing to divulge the underlying connection information.

The current supported deployment model is that endpoints aren't exposed to untrusted entities.

threats.title: Task history reset on restart
threats.description: The task history table is only kept in-memory, which means any tasks that would be captured are lost if an attacker wants to conceal what they did by either timing their activity to occur before a maintenance activity that results in a restart, or by purposefully causing the runtime to restart.
threats.mitigation: Persist task_history locally

threats.title: Expensive queries can lead to denial of service
threats.description: An attacker or misconfigured application could potentially cause a denial of service on the Spice runtime.
threats.mitigation:
Configurable limit on how much time a query can take
Deploy more Spice instances, where each Spice instance has its own resource limits

threats.title: No persistent audit logs
threats.description:
Spice does not provide audit logging of actions taken that could repudiate that a certain action was taken.
All access to Spice assumes the caller is trusted, so no identity information could be gathered even if audit logs were maintained
threats.mitigation: Implement a proper audit/task history log tracking both changes to the runtime operation (i.e. modifying Spicepod, runtime settings) as well as data operations (queries, refreshes) that is persistent across restarts.

threats.title: Data source connection details (or any secrets) leaked via errors/logging
threats.description: Metadata about connected data sources is leaked through error messages, revealing sensitive infrastructure details.
threats.mitigation: Review code where logs are emitted to ensure that potential sensitive information (i.e. credentials encoded in headers) is not leaked via error messages. Token redaction in debug/error output has been implemented. The /v1/spicepods endpoint returns summaries instead of full configuration to avoid leaking connection details.

threats.title: Excessive acceleration
threats.description: An attacker with the ability to control the Spicepod (or an unintentionally misconfigured Spicepod through legitimate means) can cause the runtime to load an acceleration that is too large to fit in-memory on the filesystem, or causes the running organization to incur excessive costs from the remote data source.

threats.title: Malicious SQL / SQL injection leading to ACE
threats.description: A user exploits a vulnerability in the SQL parser to execute arbitrary code (ACE) on the Spice runtime.
threats.mitigation: Queries that would allow modifying the state of the runtime are rejected at the parsing layer. v2.0 introduces DDL (CREATE TABLE / DROP TABLE) for Iceberg and Cayenne catalogs only; DDL is validated against an allowlist of permitted catalogs and operations. SQL identifier quoting is enforced across all connectors to prevent injection via table/column names. Prepared statements with parameterized queries are used for federated execution.

threats.title: Results caching reuse
threats.description: A malicious actor targets the results caching mechanism to retrieve sensitive data from previous queries.
threats.mitigation: Not a current threat, but could become one if we don't implement results caching with proper AuthN

threats.title: Malicious compressed small payload has unbounded/very large size
threats.description: If an attacker is able to send a payload to a Spice endpoint that is compressed, and the decompression of that payload causes Spice to run out of memory due to the payload itself having a very large/potentially unbounded size - then it could cause a denial of service. (i.e. Zipbomb)
threats.mitigation:
- No known Gzip attack vector and the HTTP endpoints only accept Gzip compression
- For connecting to data sources, we rely on object_store's implementation which should protect against this.

threats.title: Task History shows truncated results
threats.description:
If you have access to the runtime, you can access the task_history table along with some truncated outputs of data you might not normally be able to access.

This isn't a problem in v0.17.4-beta, because if you can access the task_history table, then you trivially can access any of the data sources.
threats.mitigation: No mitigation currently. Once we add AuthN/AuthZ, we will need to design how to lock this down appropriately. (i.e. RLS)

threats.title: Malicious SQL / SQL injection leading to information disclosure
threats.description: If there are functions that allow reading from the environment/file-system, this could lead to unexpected information disclosure of the system details/secrets
threats.mitigation:
- Run in a chroot process with limited file-system access
- Disable functions that allow this access

threats.title: Supply chain attack leading to compromised dependency
threats.description: If an attacker is able to compromise a dependency that we depend on, and we release a version of Spice with that compromised dependency, then all of Spice users would potentially be affected.
threats.mitigation:
- CVE scanner/dependabot to scan for known issues with dependencies
- Adopt a policy of waiting before upgrading a dependency to allow for the community to identify
- Processing scanning to identify suspicious behavior

threats.title: Unprotected control plane endpoints
threats.description: HTTP/Arrow Flight/OpenAI-compatible/MCP/Iceberg APIs accept requests without built-in authentication or rate limits by default. Exposure of these endpoints beyond a trusted network allows attackers to run arbitrary queries or inference, modify runtime state, or exfiltrate data.
threats.mitigation: Terminate traffic behind an API gateway with mTLS/JWT, restrict bind addresses/firewall rules, enable runtime-auth when available, and apply per-endpoint rate limiting before exposing services to untrusted clients.

threats.title: Prompt injection via SQL AI/LLM functions
threats.description: Model-backed SQL helpers (e.g., text-to-SQL, sql_ai, MCP tools) can be influenced by attacker-provided prompts or corpora, leading to over-broad queries, unauthorized data access, or untrusted tool execution.
threats.mitigation: Constrain AI-generated SQL to read-only allowlists, sandbox tool execution, validate model outputs, and filter/escape untrusted inputs before invoking LLM-backed functions.

threats.title: Telemetry and traces leak sensitive data
threats.description: Verbose traces, query logs, or model prompt/response bodies may include secrets or PII that are exported to OTEL/metrics backends without redaction.
threats.mitigation: Default to minimal logging, scrub sensitive fields before emission, isolate telemetry destinations, and apply retention policies/PII filtering in observability pipelines.

threats.title: Unauthorized Iceberg table writes
threats.description: The Iceberg connector supports writes while other data sources are read-only. Without strong authentication, input validation, and authorization, attackers with endpoint access can corrupt, drop, or poison Iceberg tables.
threats.mitigation: Require mTLS/JWT on write-capable endpoints, enforce schema/operation allowlists, validate write destinations, and run Iceberg connectors on isolated identities with least-privilege storage permissions.

threats.title: DDL operations allow schema manipulation
threats.description: v2.0 introduces CREATE TABLE and DROP TABLE DDL via FlightSQL and /v1/sql for Iceberg and Cayenne catalogs. An unauthenticated caller could create tables to exhaust storage, drop critical tables to cause data loss, or create tables pointing to attacker-controlled locations.
threats.mitigation: DDL is restricted to Iceberg and Cayenne catalogs configured with write mode. Deploy behind authentication (API key, mTLS). Use storage-level IAM to restrict object creation. Monitor for unexpected DDL operations via task history and tracing. Consider a DDL allowlist or approval workflow for production environments.

threats.title: Async query results readable from object storage
threats.description: Async query results are materialized to object storage for later retrieval. If the storage bucket has overly permissive ACLs, query results containing sensitive data could be accessed by unauthorized parties. Query IDs are partially predictable.
threats.mitigation: Enforce bucket-level access controls with least-privilege IAM policies. Enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3/SSE-KMS) for result artifacts. Use cryptographically random query identifiers. Apply automatic expiration/TTL on result objects. Restrict /v1/queries API access with authentication.

threats.title: Distributed ingestion allows unauthorized data writes
threats.description: In v2.0, distributed ingestion allows executor nodes to write data to accelerated tables (including Cayenne). A compromised or rogue executor could inject malicious data, corrupt accelerated tables, or overwrite legitimate data during distributed ingestion.
threats.mitigation: Restrict executor registration to trusted nodes via allowlisting. Run cluster communication over private networks or with mTLS. Validate ingested data schemas before commit. Use Cayenne's WAL-based staged writes to detect and roll back partial/corrupt ingestions. Monitor for data anomalies post-ingestion.

threats.title: Cayenne WAL poisoning or corruption
threats.description: Cayenne's staged append writes use a WAL (Write-Ahead Log) for atomicity. If an attacker gains filesystem access, they could modify WAL files to inject or corrupt data that will be committed on the next WAL flush. Partial WAL recovery after crash could also surface inconsistent state.
threats.mitigation: Restrict filesystem permissions on Cayenne data directories (mode 600). Run Spice as a least-privileged user. Validate WAL entries against expected schemas before commit. Implement WAL integrity checksums. Use S3 Express One Zone with IAM for remote storage instead of local filesystem when possible.

threats.title: DuckLake catalog metadata manipulation
threats.description: The DuckLake catalog stores metadata in DuckDB with data files in object storage. If attackers gain access to the DuckDB metadata database, they could redirect table references to malicious Parquet files, alter schema definitions, or manipulate time-travel snapshots to serve poisoned historical data.
threats.mitigation: Restrict access to the DuckDB metadata database file via filesystem permissions. Use encrypted connections to the metadata store. Validate Parquet file checksums on read. Run Spice with least-privilege storage credentials that scope access to the intended bucket prefix. Audit metadata changes.

threats.title: GCS credential exposure via data connector
threats.description: The GCS data connector (Alpha) requires Google Cloud credentials for bucket access. Service account keys or application default credentials could be leaked through error messages, verbose logging, or Spicepod configuration stored in version control.
threats.mitigation: Use Workload Identity Federation instead of long-lived service account keys. Store credentials in runtime-secrets, not in Spicepod YAML. Review error handling to ensure credential material is not logged. Apply least-privilege IAM roles scoped to specific buckets/prefixes.

threats.title: URL Tables enable SQL-level SSRF
threats.description: When URL Tables are enabled (runtime.params.url_tables: enabled), any authenticated user can issue SQL queries against arbitrary URLs (S3, Azure Blob, HTTP/HTTPS), e.g. SELECT * FROM 's3://internal-bucket/secrets.parquet' or SELECT * FROM 'https://internal-api/data'. This uses Spice's ambient cloud credentials (IAM role, service account), allowing users to access resources reachable by the runtime but not authorized for the user. This is the most significant SSRF vector in the system.
threats.mitigation: URL Tables are opt-in (disabled by default). Only enable in trusted environments. Deploy behind authentication (API key, mTLS). Consider implementing URL allowlists/blocklists for permitted URL patterns. Scope runtime IAM credentials to only required data sources. Monitor queries for unexpected URL patterns via task history.

threats.title: SMB/NFS connectors expose internal network storage
threats.description: The SMB and NFS data connectors allow Spice to access network-attached storage. If an attacker can influence Spicepod configuration or has DDL access, they could point datasets to internal file shares (smb://internal-fileserver/sensitive-share/) to exfiltrate data. SMB credentials (smb_username/smb_password) are stored in runtime-secrets and held in memory. NFS relies on host-level permissions with no application-level authentication.
threats.mitigation: Restrict Spicepod modification to trusted operators. Validate SMB/NFS URIs against an allowlist of permitted hosts/shares. Store SMB credentials in runtime-secrets, not in Spicepod YAML. Review error handling to ensure SMB credentials are not leaked in logs. Apply network-level ACLs to restrict Spice's access to only intended NAS endpoints.

threats.title: Acceleration snapshot rollback serves stale data
threats.description: The POST /v1/datasets/{dataset}/acceleration/snapshots/current endpoint allows rolling back to a previous snapshot. A malicious client with API access could roll back to stale or outdated data without authorization, causing the system to serve incorrect results. Repeated snapshot creation could also exhaust disk or object storage.
threats.mitigation: Deploy behind authentication (API key, mTLS) to restrict snapshot management to authorized operators. Monitor for unexpected snapshot rollback operations via task history and tracing. Apply storage quotas to limit snapshot accumulation. Consider separating snapshot management from query endpoints with distinct authorization policies.

threats.title: Unauthenticated Prometheus metrics exposure
threats.description: The Prometheus metrics endpoint on port 9090 has no authentication or mTLS. An attacker with network access can scrape all runtime metrics, revealing query patterns, dataset sizes, error rates, acceleration refresh timings, executor counts, and other operational details that could inform targeted attacks.
threats.mitigation: Restrict network access to port 9090 via firewall rules or Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Deploy a reverse proxy with authentication in front of the metrics endpoint if exposure to untrusted networks is required. Use Kubernetes pod-level network policies to limit scraping access to the monitoring system only.

data.name: Spice Cluster (Scheduler/Executors)
data.description: Ballista-based distributed query execution over gRPC with built-in mTLS on internal port 50052. v2.0 adds active-active HA via object-store-based scheduler registry, partition-aware data distribution with greedy set cover executor selection, ExpandSecret RPC for secret forwarding, bidirectional control streams, and distributed ingestion.

threats.title: Man-in-the-middle Data Sources
threats.description: A potential man-in-the-middle attack is possible where an attacker can inject themselves in the middle of the data source data stream to modify data in transit, causing Spice to return attacker-controlled payloads to the client applications.
threats.mitigation:
Connect to remote data sources using TLS/SSL
For data connectors that don't support TLS (FTP, Debezium) - connect over a secure network instead.

threats.title: Unauthenticated Iceberg write path abuse
threats.description: Because Iceberg supports writes, a compromised or unauthenticated caller could alter, overwrite, or delete Iceberg tables via the data connector.
threats.mitigation: Enforce authentication/authorization for Iceberg write endpoints, isolate Iceberg credentials, and apply storage-level ACLs and table-level governance.

threats.title: Model gateway key leakage and unbounded spend
threats.description: Hosted model and embedding providers are called with API keys. A compromised runtime, verbose logs, or replay of this channel can expose keys or allow attackers to trigger costly inference at scale.
threats.mitigation: Store provider keys in runtime-secrets, avoid logging headers/bodies, enforce egress allowlists and rate limits, and rotate provider credentials regularly.

data.name: Cluster Control Plane
data.description: gRPC communication between the Spice runtime and the Ballista scheduler, and between scheduler and executors. Network connections are executor-initiated (executor connects to scheduler); the gRPC stream itself is bidirectional for carrying commands and metrics. Includes SchedulerGrpcServer (Ballista task dispatch) and ClusterService (GetAppDefinition, ExpandSecret RPCs). Previously, GetAppDefinition and ExpandSecret were Flight Actions on the public port (50051); they are now served only on the internal mTLS-protected port (50052).

threats.title: Rogue cluster node injection
threats.description: Ballista scheduler and executor communication occurs over gRPC on a dedicated internal port (50052). Without mTLS enabled, a malicious host on the network could register a fake executor, intercept ExpandSecret RPCs to steal secrets, inject UpdatePartitions control-stream commands to reassign data, or read query data in transit. v2.0 increases risk: active-active HA with scheduler registry in object storage and dynamic cluster sizing mean executors join/leave frequently, and distributed ingestion allows executors to write data, not just read it.
threats.mitigation: Enable built-in mTLS (--node-mtls-ca-certificate-file, --node-mtls-certificate-file, --node-mtls-key-file), which is required by default for cluster mode (opt-out only via --allow-insecure-connections). Keep cluster traffic on a private network, restrict scheduler/executor discovery to allowlisted peers, and disable the cluster feature when not required.

threats.title: Control stream hijacking
threats.description: The bidirectional gRPC control stream between scheduler and executor carries privileged commands: UpdatePartitions (reassign data ownership), CancelTasks (abort query execution), PollNow (trigger immediate task polling), and Heartbeat (maintain session liveness). Without mTLS, an attacker could inject control-stream messages to reassign partitions to attacker-controlled nodes, cancel legitimate queries, or spoof heartbeats to keep stale sessions alive.
threats.mitigation: Enable built-in mTLS to authenticate both sides of the control stream. Deploy control-stream endpoints on the internal port (50052) not reachable from external networks. Monitor for unexpected control-stream commands via cluster observability. Implement command-level validation and rate limiting on the scheduler side.

data.name: Data Source(s)
data.description: Represents any number of data sources that Spice can connect to, including new GCS (Alpha) and DuckLake catalog connectors in v2.0.

data.name: Cayenne Accelerator (Vortex + SQLite)
data.description: Multi-file acceleration format combining Vortex columnar data and SQLite metadata. v2.0 RC adds staged WAL writes, DDL support, and distributed ingestion.

threats.title: Tampering with file-based accelerators
threats.description: Modifying file-based accelerators (DuckDB, SQLite, Cayenne Vortex files, DuckLake metadata) to inject malicious content. v2.0 increases the surface area with Cayenne WAL files and DuckLake DuckDB metadata on the local filesystem.
threats.mitigation:
- Run Spice as a least privileged user.
- Run application with least privilege, ideally without file-system access.
- Restrict Cayenne data directory and DuckLake metadata permissions to mode 600.

threats.title: Bypass underlying data source AuthN/AuthZ by reading accelerator files
threats.description: When Spice is configured to accelerate data from a data source to a file (i.e. DuckDB/SQLite/Cayenne) then its possible to bypass all AuthN/AuthZ measures if the attacker has access to the file.
threats.mitigation:
- Limit the file permissions to only the user running the Spice instance
  - [Action]: Change default file permission to 600
  - [Action]: Configuration to allow changing permission
- Instead of running Spice on the same machine, run it in a separate machine in the trusted network.
- chroot the Spice instance AND chroot the application

threats.title: Tampering with the Spicepod
threats.description: If an attacker can access/modify the Spicepod, they can tamper with how the Spice runtime loads data sources and potentially point them to data sources that the attacker controls, to disrupt/poison the operations of applications configured to query this Spice instance.
threats.mitigation:
- Proper file permissions so that only the Spice instance can access the Spicepod.
- [Action]: Update deployment examples to limit file permissions of Spicepod.

data.name: Hosted Model Provider
data.description: Third-party LLM/embedding APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, x.ai, etc.).

data.name: Acceleration Snapshots / Object Storage
data.description: Remote S3/GCS/object storage for snapshot bootstrap, Cayenne/Vortex artifacts, async query results (Arrow IPC chunks with 12h default TTL), DuckLake data files, scheduler registry records ({prefix}/schedulers/{id}.json), job state ({prefix}/jobs/{job_id}.json), and partition metadata ({prefix}/accelerations/partitions/{table}.json). Uses ETag-based optimistic concurrency control (OCC) for state coordination.

threats.title: Unsigned acceleration snapshots or artifacts
threats.description: Acceleration snapshots, Vortex files, async query result artifacts, or DuckLake Parquet files fetched from external object storage can be replaced or poisoned, leading to corrupted query results or malicious payload execution paths.
threats.mitigation: Serve artifacts from access-controlled buckets, validate checksums/signatures before load, pin expected digests, and run the runtime as a least-privileged user with read-only mounts.

threats.title: Scheduler registry poisoning via object storage
threats.description: The active-active scheduler registry stores scheduler records at {prefix}/schedulers/{id}.json in object storage with heartbeat TTL. An attacker with write access to the object storage bucket could inject a fake scheduler record pointing to an attacker-controlled endpoint, causing executors to connect to a malicious scheduler that could intercept queries, steal secrets via ExpandSecret responses, or issue malicious control-stream commands.
threats.mitigation: Restrict object storage write access to scheduler nodes via IAM policies scoped to the registry prefix. Use ETag-based OCC to detect unauthorized writes. Enable bucket versioning and object lock. Monitor for unexpected scheduler records. Validate scheduler TLS certificates when mTLS is enabled.

threats.title: Partition metadata tampering in object storage
threats.description: Partition assignments are stored at {prefix}/accelerations/partitions/{table}.json in object storage. An attacker with write access could modify partition assignments to redirect data reads to attacker-controlled executors, remove partitions to cause data loss, or reassign partitions to overload specific executors (denial of service). The ETag-based OCC mechanism prevents concurrent legitimate modifications but does not authenticate writers.
threats.mitigation: Restrict write access to partition metadata prefixes via IAM policies. Enable bucket versioning for audit trail. Use checksums to validate partition metadata integrity. Monitor for unexpected partition reassignments. Alert on partition metadata modifications outside of normal scheduler operations.

data.name: Ballista Scheduler
data.description: Distributes query fragments and ingestion tasks to executors. v2.0 adds active-active HA via a scheduler registry in object storage ({prefix}/schedulers/{id}.json with heartbeat TTL). Manages partition assignments ({prefix}/accelerations/partitions/), serves secrets to executors via ExpandSecret RPC, and broadcasts UpdatePartitions/PollNow commands over bidirectional gRPC control streams. Listens on internal port 50052 (mTLS-protected by default).

threats.title: Secret forwarding interception via ExpandSecret RPC
threats.description: The scheduler serves secret values to executors via the ExpandSecret gRPC RPC on the internal port (50052). Secrets are transmitted in cleartext within the gRPC payload. Without mTLS, an attacker with network access could intercept ExpandSecret responses to capture data source credentials, API keys, and other secrets held in the scheduler's secret store.
threats.mitigation: Enable built-in mTLS for cluster communication (required by default; opt-out only via --allow-insecure-connections). Restrict network access to port 50052. Apply least-privilege secret scoping so executors only receive secrets required for their assigned partitions. Rotate secrets regularly. Monitor ExpandSecret call patterns for anomalies.

threats.title: GetAppDefinition RPC exposes full Spicepod configuration
threats.description: The GetAppDefinition RPC on the ClusterService (internal port 50052) returns the full Spicepod configuration to executors, including all dataset definitions, connection parameters, and runtime settings. Without mTLS, an attacker with network access to port 50052 could call GetAppDefinition to obtain the full application configuration, which may contain or reference sensitive connection details. Previously this was exposed as a Flight Action on the public port (50051); it was moved to the internal ClusterService as a critical security improvement.
threats.mitigation: Enable built-in mTLS to restrict GetAppDefinition to authenticated cluster members only. Ensure port 50052 is not exposed to untrusted networks. Monitor for unexpected GetAppDefinition calls. Consider minimizing the configuration returned to executors to only the data they need for their assigned partitions.

data.name: Ballista Executor
data.description: Executes query fragments and, in v2.0, performs distributed data ingestion into accelerated tables including Cayenne. Retrieves secrets from the scheduler via ExpandSecret RPC (secrets are never stored locally). Receives partition assignments and control commands (UpdatePartitions, CancelTasks) over a bidirectional gRPC control stream. Reports metrics back to the scheduler through the same control stream.

threats.title: Executor data exfiltration via distributed ingestion
threats.description: v2.0 executors now perform distributed ingestion, reading from data sources and writing to accelerated tables. A compromised executor could exfiltrate source data during ingestion, or redirect writes to an attacker-controlled destination.
threats.mitigation: Restrict executor network egress to only required data sources and object storage. Use IAM roles/instance profiles scoped to specific resources. Audit executor activity via cluster observability metrics. Run executors in isolated network segments.

threats.title: Shuffle data exposure in executor memory or storage
threats.description: During distributed query execution, intermediate shuffle data (partial query results exchanged between executors) is held in executor memory, local disk, or object storage in Arrow IPC or Vortex format. A compromised executor or an attacker with access to the executor's filesystem or object storage prefix could read sensitive intermediate results that would not otherwise be accessible.
threats.mitigation: Enable mTLS for all inter-executor data exchange (Flight shuffle). Use encrypted local storage for shuffle spill files. Apply short TTLs and automatic cleanup for shuffle artifacts in object storage. Restrict executor filesystem access and object storage prefixes with least-privilege IAM.

data.name: DuckLake Metadata (DuckDB)
data.description: DuckDB-backed metadata catalog for DuckLake lakehouse tables. Stores table schemas, file references, and snapshot history for time travel. New in v2.0.

data.name: Async Query Results
data.description: Async query results materialized to and retrieved from object storage.

threats.title: Async query result tampering in object storage
threats.description: Async query results written to object storage could be modified by an attacker with bucket access before the client retrieves them, leading to the client consuming corrupted or malicious data.
threats.mitigation: Enable bucket versioning and object lock. Use server-side encryption. Apply least-privilege IAM policies. Validate checksums on retrieval. Use pre-signed URLs with short TTLs for result retrieval.

diagrams.description: Models the components involved in federated query, acceleration, LLM inference, DDL operations, async query execution, and distributed execution for the Spice runtime v2.0.
